beats.narration_text: Hi — I'm Divij Pawar. Two agents look at the exact same evidence — same filing, same numbers, same question — and come back with opposite answers. Agent A is confident the company's margins are improving. Agent B is just as confident they're not. Both wrote clean, well-reasoned explanations. Both cited real sources. Neither one is lying — they just can't both be right. Today: what actually happens the second two agents disagree, and why the instinctive fix — average their answers and move on — is about the worst thing you could do.

props.command: What actually happens when two AI agents disagree?
output: Agent A: margins improving. Agent B: margins declining.
Averaging the two doesn't get you closer to the truth
The disagreement itself is the signal worth keeping

beats.act: the naive fix, and why it's wrong
beats.narration_text: The obvious move is to blend the outputs — average the two confidence scores, split the difference on the conclusion, ship something moderate and hedged, and move on. That instinct is exactly wrong. Averaging two agents who disagree doesn't get you closer to the truth — it gets you an answer that looks moderate but is really nobody's actual opinion. If Agent A is right and Agent B is wrong, blending them just makes the true answer worse. And it throws away the one piece of information in the whole exchange that was actually valuable: the fact that they disagreed at all. A controller that quietly smooths conflicting outputs into a neutral-sounding grade has taken the most informative moment in the pipeline and erased it.

shot.visual_intent: Two contradicting speech bubbles get fed into a blender and come out as one grey, wishy-washy bubble — then the same blend is shown against the case where Agent A was actually right, so the viewer sees averaging make the true answer worse, not better.

show.event: Two speech bubbles — ink 'margins improving', terracotta 'margins declining' — seat side by side, both pointing at one shared document
Both bubbles slide into a blender icon at center
The blender spins; a single grey bubble emerges reading 'results may vary'
A second row plays: Agent A's bubble is marked 'right', Agent B's marked 'wrong'; the blended grey bubble sits visibly further from A's position than A's own answer was
A serif landing line holds: 'erases the one fact that mattered: they disagreed'

beats.narration_text: So: treat disagreement between independent agents as a signal, not noise, and don't blend it away. Detect it on structure — confidence and direction — not wording. Bound the debate to a single round. And if it's still unresolved, it has to reach the final output looking unresolved, not smoothed into one grade. It lowers your risk. It doesn't take it to zero.

artifactLines: Disagreement between independent agents is a signal, not noise
Detect it on structure — confidence and direction — not wording
Bound the debate to one round, or tone starts beating correctness
Unresolved has to reach the final output looking unresolved

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Look at a system you're building or using with more than one agent — even two steps that each produce a judgment. First, name the structured signal you'd actually compare if they disagreed: a confidence score, a directional call, not the raw text. Second, pick a threshold — how big a gap actually counts as a real disagreement, versus just different phrasing. Third, decide, before it ever happens, what your system does with 'unresolved' — where it shows up, and who sees it first.

props.command: Where could two of my own agents actually disagree?
output: Name the structured signal you'd compare — confidence + direction
Pick a threshold: how big a gap counts as a real disagreement
Decide what 'unresolved' looks like before it ever happens
